## The question

F04 asked whether HR and LR *differ*. This asks something stricter: given a
subject the model has never seen, can it say which arm they belong to?

The two questions come apart. A difference can be real and still useless for
assignment if the groups overlap. And a classifier that separates the sixteen
subjects it was fitted on tells you nothing, because with 1,900 features and 16
subjects a perfect boundary always exists. Only the out-of-sample number counts.

## Out of sample

### The idea

Hold one subject out. Fit everything — scaling, feature selection, tuning — on
the other fifteen. Predict the held-out subject once. Put them back and repeat
for all sixteen. Each subject is predicted exactly once, by a model that never
saw them.

The subject, not the sample, is the unit. Holding out a *sample* would leave that
person's other two biopsies in the training set, and the model could learn to
recognise the person rather than the arm.

### Formally

Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. For subjects $s = 1,\dots,n$ with
features $x_s$ and label $y_s \in \{0,1\}$:

$$
\hat{y}_s = f_{-s}(x_s),
\qquad
f_{-s} = \arg\min_{f} \sum_{k \neq s} L\big(y_k, f(x_k)\big) + \lambda\,\Omega(f)
$$

The subscript $-s$ carries the whole point: every transform and every
hyperparameter is estimated from the other $n-1$ subjects.

### Nested, not flat

Each model has a tuning parameter — the penalty $\lambda$ in elastic net, the
number of components in sparse PLS-DA, the shrinkage in nearest shrunken
centroids. Choosing it by looking at all sixteen subjects and then reporting LOSO
accuracy leaks the held-out subject into the model that predicts them.

So tuning runs in an **inner** cross-validation over the fifteen training
subjects, inside each of the sixteen outer folds. That is what nested means, and
it is the difference between an honest estimate and a flattering one.

### The three leakage traps

| Trap | Why it leaks | What is done |
|---|---|---|
| Scaling on the full matrix | The held-out subject shapes the centre and scale | Scaling fitted on training subjects, applied to the held-out one |
| Feature selection before the loop | Features chosen because they separate all sixteen | Selection inside each fold |
| WGCNA modules defined cohort-wide | Module membership saw every subject | Flagged on the figure as an optimistic upper bound; `04_Features/modules/loso_refit` measures what in-fold redefinition costs |

The module level is the honest weak point. Eigengenes are defined once across the
whole cohort, so that arm is an upper bound rather than a clean out-of-sample
number.

## Scoring

### The idea

Each subject comes out with a predicted probability of being HR. AUC asks: pick
one real HR and one real LR at random; how often does the model give the HR the
higher score? Chance is 0.5, perfect is 1.

AUC rather than accuracy, because it does not depend on where the threshold is
put.

### Formally

$$
\mathrm{AUC} = \frac{1}{n_1 n_0}\sum_{i:\,y_i=1}\ \sum_{j:\,y_j=0}
\Big[ \mathbf{1}(\hat{p}_i > \hat{p}_j) + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{1}(\hat{p}_i = \hat{p}_j) \Big]
$$

the Mann–Whitney U statistic scaled to $[0,1]$.

## The null

### The idea

At sixteen subjects an AUC of 0.70 sounds good and means very little. To find
out, destroy the labels and see what the same machinery produces from noise:
shuffle the HR/LR assignment across subjects, rerun the entire nested loop,
record the AUC. Two hundred times gives the distribution of AUCs this design
yields when there is nothing to find.

The whole loop reruns each time, not just the final fit. Permuting after feature
selection would pit a tuned model against an untuned null.

### Formally

With observed statistic $T$ and replicates $T^{(1)},\dots,T^{(B)}$,

$$
\hat{p} = \frac{1 + \#\{b : T^{(b)} \ge T\}}{B + 1}
$$

The $+1$ in both places is not cosmetic: it stops $\hat p$ ever being exactly
zero, which would claim more resolution than $B$ replicates support. At
$B = 200$ the smallest reportable $p$ is $1/201 \approx 0.005$.

### A lead is two conditions

```{r}
#| label: lead-def
LEAD_BASELINE
```

A cell is a **lead** only when `perm_p < .05` **and** its AUC beats 0.5. Both are
needed. Ridge and the unpenalised model collapse their nulls — every shuffle
returns nearly the same AUC — so a small $p$ can arrive attached to an AUC
*below* chance. `is_lead()` in `functions/sweep_grid.R` is the one definition
every count, panel and curve reads, so the manifest, the roll-up and the
composite cannot disagree.

### Why so many cells score AUC exactly 0

Half the cells in this screen report an AUC of exactly 0.000, and that number
means the opposite of what it looks like.

When a penalised model finds no signal it shrinks to the intercept, and its
prediction becomes the training set's class proportion. Under leave-one-subject-
out, removing a subject shifts that proportion **against** them. In a cell with
7 HR and 8 LR: hold out an HR subject and the model trains on 6 HR of 14, so it
predicts 0.4286; hold out an LR subject and it trains on 7 of 14, predicting
0.500 or more.

Every HR is therefore scored lower than every LR, and the ranking is perfectly
inverted:

```{r}
#| label: loso-inversion
#| echo: false
read.xlsx(
  here(
    "05_Figures", "F05_classification", "modules", "acute", "HR_LR", "ridge",
    "c_data", "results.xlsx"
  ),
  "predictions"
) |>
  mutate(arm = ifelse(.data$y == 1, "HR", "LR")) |>
  summarise(
    n = dplyr::n(), distinct_predictions = dplyr::n_distinct(round(.data$pred, 6)),
    min = round(min(.data$pred), 4), max = round(max(.data$pred), 4),
    .by = "arm"
  )
```

Three distinct predicted values across fifteen subjects. The model is a constant
plus the arithmetic of its own cross-validation.

**AUC = 0 means no signal, not inverted signal.** It follows that the median AUC
across this screen — well below 0.5 — is not evidence that the proteome predicts
worse than chance. It is evidence that most cells found nothing.

Two things in the design already handle it. The permutation null suffers the
identical pathology, since shuffled labels also produce intercept-only fits, so
the null is centred near zero too and the comparison stays valid. And the
baseline condition (AUC > 0.5) is exactly the guard that stops an intercept-only
cell being promoted by a small $p$. This is the clearest argument in the pipeline
for why neither the null nor the baseline is optional.

## The screen

The pipeline does not fit one classifier. It fits every combination of:

```{r}
#| label: grid
#| echo: false
tibble::tibble(
  axis = c("feature level", "timepoint config", "model"),
  values = c(
    paste(SWEEP_LEVELS, collapse = ", "),
    paste(SWEEP_CONFIGS, collapse = ", "),
    paste(c(CLASS_METHODS, PLAIN_METHOD), collapse = ", ")
  )
)
```

That is 153 cells. Reporting the best without saying how many were tried is the
garden of forking paths [@phillips2013]: with 153 draws the maximum is large
even when every cell is noise.

### Why there is no BH q here

BH controls the false discovery rate over a family of tests. These 153 are not a
family in the sense BH needs — they share subjects, they nest inside each other
(`total` contains `training` and `acute`), and they reuse overlapping feature
spaces. A q across them would assert an independence structure that is absent.

The honest alternative is what the figure does: report the raw permutation $p$,
report the screen size beside it, and show the whole distribution of cells rather
than the winner alone.

## The figure

![F05 classification composite](../b_reports/F05_classification_composite.png)

- **A** The twelve cells with the smallest permutation $p$, each a filled ROC
  curve keyed to feature level, with AUC, its interval and the permutation $p$.
  A bold border marks nominal $p<.05$.
- **B** The specification curve: all 153 cells sorted by AUC against their own
  permutation-null bands, with a strip below reading off level, config and
  method.

Panel B is the one that matters. A real effect appears as a cluster of cells
lifting above their null bands together, robust to which analytical choice you
make. Noise appears as a smooth sweep crossing its band about as often as chance
predicts.

## The result

```{r}
#| label: result
#| echo: false
read.xlsx(
  here("05_Figures", "F05_classification", "c_data", "results.xlsx"),
  "all_cells"
) |>
  best_b_per_cell() |>
  summarise(
    cells = dplyr::n(),
    median_auc = round(median(.data$estimate, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    max_auc = round(max(.data$estimate, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    leads = sum(is_lead(.data$estimate, .data$perm_p, "class"), na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = "level"
  )
```

Zero leads of 153. At a 5% chance rate a screen this size would be expected to
throw up roughly eight cells clearing $p<.05$ by luck alone. It produced fewer
than chance.

The proteome does not classify responder status out of sample at this cohort
size, under any feature level, timepoint encoding or algorithm tried.

## How to read this honestly

A null classification at $n = 16$ has two possible causes and this design cannot
separate them: there is no signal, or there is signal too small for sixteen
subjects to reveal. What the screen does establish is that the answer does not
turn on the analytical choice — no combination of level, config and model
rescues it, which is a stronger statement than any single model failing.

The complementary caution: a lead, had one appeared, would still need replication
in an independent cohort before being called a classifier. A screen maximum is a
hypothesis, not a result.

## Recap

- The subject is the unit of cross-validation, never the sample.
- Tuning happens inside each fold, or the estimate flatters itself.
- The permutation null reruns the whole loop, not just the final fit.
- A lead needs a small $p$ **and** a metric above the trivial baseline.
- 153 cells, no BH q, because they are not an independent family.
- 0 of 153 qualify.
